UNIT 7: EARTHQUAKES - CAUSES, EFFECTS, PREPARATION AND RESPONSE

KEY THEME
- Earthquakes are sudden movements of the Earth's crust caused by the release of energy along faults or plate boundaries.
- Learning outcomes: identify the key features of an earthquake from a diagram; explain where and why earthquakes occur; describe causes and effects in a Global North (Japan) and Global South (Indonesia) setting; understand monitoring, preparing and planning to lessen effects; assess preparation and response by comparing the two case studies.

KEY TERMS
- Seismology: the study of earthquakes - how and why they happen, how they are measured and their effects. Seismologists study seismic waves, fault lines and tectonic processes to better predict earthquakes and reduce their impact.
- Earthquake: a vibration of the Earth's surface caused by a sudden movement along a fault.
- Fault: a crack in the Earth's surface where the risk of earthquakes may be higher. It is where bumping and sliding happens along plate boundaries. Plate boundaries can have many faults.
- Focus: the point where the earthquake starts. It is deep under the ground, inside the Earth's crust.
- Epicentre: the place on the Earth's surface directly above the focus. Effects are felt most strongly here.
- Seismic waves: shock waves that spread out from the focus. They get weaker the further they are from the epicentre.
- Benioff zone: found at convergent boundaries where an oceanic plate subducts beneath a continental or another oceanic plate. Earthquakes here can be shallow (0-70 km), intermediate (70-300 km) or deep (300-700 km).
- Shearing: the sideways movement of two plates sliding past each other at a transform boundary.
- Moment Magnitude Scale: describes the total energy released by an earthquake. It has replaced the Richter scale for medium to large earthquakes because it is more accurate, especially for very strong or deep events where the Richter scale underestimates size.
- Mercalli scale: shows the intensity of shaking and visible damage at specific places, from I (not felt) to XII (total destruction).
- Liquefaction: water-saturated soil loses strength and acts like a liquid, so buildings tilt, sink or collapse.
- Thrust faulting: movement where one block of land is forced upwards over another.
- Strike-slip fault: plates slide past each other rather than moving into or away from one another; movement is mostly horizontal.

COMPONENTS OF AN EARTHQUAKE (Figure 7.1 in words)
- Deep in the crust is the focus. Seismic waves spread out in rings from the focus. Directly above it on the surface is the epicentre. A fault line runs through the crust to the surface (where there can be surface rupture).
- SEC sample question: labels A epicentre, B seismic waves, C fault line, D focus.

WHERE EARTHQUAKES OCCUR
- At convergent, divergent and transform plate boundaries.

CONVERGENT PLATE BOUNDARIES
- Two plates move towards each other and collide, creating intense pressure and stress.
- One plate subducts (slides under) the other - often the oceanic plate, because it is denser than the continental plate.
- Rocks and crust bend, twist and break along the subduction zone (intense rock deformation). This creates friction and stress builds up.
- When stress becomes too great for the rocks, it is released suddenly as energy - an earthquake.
- Example: the Nazca Plate and South American Plate collide along the Peru-Chile Trench; the denser oceanic Nazca Plate is forced under the less dense continental South American Plate.
- The subduction zone has frequent, powerful earthquakes in the Benioff zone, at various depths in the subducting plate. This makes convergent boundaries some of the most seismically active places on Earth.
- Diagram (Fig 7.2): oceanic crust subducting under continental crust at the trench; shallow earthquakes near the surface, deep earthquakes further down the sinking plate.
- 1960 Valdivia earthquake, Chile: the largest ever recorded, magnitude 9.5. Catastrophic damage, massive tsunamis that crossed the Pacific, about 2 million people homeless, over 1,600 deaths in Chile alone.

DIVERGENT PLATE BOUNDARIES
- Two plates move apart, so the crust stretches and eventually cracks.
- Magma rises from the mantle to fill the gaps and forms new crust (rocks melt as pressure is released).
- Stretching and breaking make the crust thin and brittle, giving shallow earthquakes, usually less than 30 km deep. They have a low magnitude but happen often.
- Example: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge on the Atlantic floor. It separates the Eurasian and North American plates in the North Atlantic and the African and South American plates in the South Atlantic. Shallow earthquakes occur along it as new oceanic crust forms, mostly along the middle of the ridge (rift zone). Iceland sits on it.
- Slow-moving mantle currents in the asthenosphere drive the movement.

TRANSFORM PLATE BOUNDARIES
- Two plates slide past each other sideways along a fault line (shearing). Movement is mostly horizontal, so no crust is made or destroyed.
- Friction makes the plates get stuck in places; pressure builds over time. When the shearing force becomes stronger than the friction, the plates jolt forward, releasing energy as an earthquake.
- These earthquakes are shallow (the shearing happens close to the surface). Because the focus is near the surface they have a high magnitude and are very destructive - the energy has only a short distance to travel to where people live.
- Example: the San Andreas Fault, California. The Pacific Plate moves north-west relative to the North American Plate. It caused the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.

EFFECTS OF EARTHQUAKES
- Ground shaking: the most direct effect. Buildings, bridges and structures sway or collapse. Severity depends on magnitude, distance and ground conditions. (Photo: Port-au-Prince, Haiti.)
- Structural damage: collapse of buildings and bridges causes injuries and deaths; falling debris and glass add risk. (Photo: Sichuan earthquake.)
- Ground rupture: ground movement breaks and visibly shifts the surface, damaging roads, pipelines and infrastructure.
- Landslides and mass movement: shaking loosens rocks and soil, triggering landslides that may bury roads, homes or communities. (Photo: Bogo Bay earthquake.)
- Liquefaction: water-saturated soil acts like a liquid; structures tilt, sink or collapse.
- Fires: broken gas lines and electrical wiring start fires that are hard to control if water systems are damaged. (Photo: Padang, Sumatra earthquake.)
- Floods: damage to dams and levees leads to severe flooding downstream.
- Tsunamis: large underwater earthquakes displace a large volume of water, making huge waves. Waves move outward in all directions at up to 800 km per hour. They gain height in shallow water and crash onto the shore, devastating low-lying coasts.
- Disruption of services: damage to water, power, sewage and communication systems; roads and bridges destroyed; emergency response slowed. (Photo: LA earthquake.)
- Human impacts: injuries, deaths, displacement, emotional stress and financial loss, worst for vulnerable people and places with weak infrastructure. (Photo: Palu, Central Sulawesi.)

PREPARING FOR AND RESPONDING TO EARTHQUAKES
- Short-term preparation and response: being ready for the moments before, during and just after an earthquake - emergency preparedness, rapid response systems and monitoring to give early warnings and organise rescue quickly.
- Long-term preparation and response: keeping people safe in future and helping recovery over months and years - earthquake-resistant construction and continuous monitoring.

EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS (earthquakes are unpredictable, so planning before, during and after is crucial)
- Emergency action plans: clear evacuation plans and practice drills for homes, schools and workplaces, with meeting points, routes and roles. Example: the annual ShakeOut drill worldwide (from the US) practises 'Drop, Cover and Hold On'.
- Emergency kits: food, water, first aid, torches, batteries and important documents for at least three days - standard advice in places like Japan.
- Securing the environment: screw heavy furniture and appliances to walls, store heavy or breakable items low down, repair structural weaknesses. Many homes and offices in Japan fix bookcases to walls.
- Family and community communication: a family plan such as a phone group; children take part in school drills. Japanese schools hold regular drills and teach children how to reunite with family.

EARLY WARNING (RAPID RESPONSE) SYSTEMS
- Detect seismic activity and send alerts to areas likely to be hit, usually seconds before shaking arrives (depending on distance from the epicentre).
- Allows people to take cover, trains to slow or stop, and automatic valves to shut gas lines and power plants.
- Tsunami alerts usually give more time for coastal people to evacuate to higher ground.
- Shake maps show shaking intensity at specific locations, give quick estimates of magnitude and likely damage; emergency services use them to decide where rescue is needed most.
- Automatic systems can close bridges, shut down factory machinery or set off alarms, preventing secondary disasters.
- In Japan, alerts go to mobile phones; early warning has let trains stop and people take cover, reducing casualties.

MONITORING SEISMIC ACTIVITY
- Seismometers: placed in the ground to detect and record vibrations. They turn vibrations into electrical signals shown as seismograms. Modern ones use three sensors (up-down, east-west, north-south) to pinpoint location and magnitude.
- Seismic networks: groups of connected seismometers across regions or countries give more accurate location and strength in real time, e.g. the US Geological Survey.
- Accelerometers: measure how quickly the ground moves, helping to assess likely damage.
- Satellites: spot ground shifts, cracks and deformation from space.
- Computer analysis: computers quickly analyse data to locate earthquakes and estimate size; GIS and digital mapping give interactive spatial analysis.

EARTHQUAKE-RESISTANT CONSTRUCTION (long term)
- Base isolation: flexible pads or bearings under the building let it sway gently, separate from the ground shaking, reducing the movement passed into the building.
- Damping systems: dampers absorb and control vibrations to keep the building stable. The Yokohama Landmark Tower has large dampers high up.
- Reinforced structures and flexible frames: reinforced concrete, steel and wood bend without breaking. Many Japanese houses use wood; the Yokohama Tower has strong steel frames.
- Building shape and design: simple, symmetrical shapes (square or rectangular) spread seismic energy evenly; irregular shapes are more likely to twist or collapse. After the 2011 Tohoku earthquake, Japanese schools and public buildings were built with simple symmetrical shapes and central safety areas.

GLOBAL NORTH vs GLOBAL SOUTH
- Severity depends on building strength and quality of emergency response. Wealthier countries usually limit impacts; poorer countries may face more destruction and casualties.

CASE STUDY: NOTO EARTHQUAKE, JAPAN, 2024 (GLOBAL NORTH)
Cause:
- The Noto Peninsula is near a convergent boundary where the Okhotsk Plate and Amur Plate move towards each other. Pressure built up and in January 2024 caused sudden movement along faults - a magnitude 7.6 earthquake.
- Thrust faulting: one block of land forced up over another. Ground lifted by up to 5 m in places. The shape and position of the faults made the effects stronger.
Effects:
- At least 645 deaths, mostly in Ishikawa Prefecture. Many died when homes collapsed; others from hypothermia, stress from aftershocks, living in shelters or disrupted medical care, especially the elderly.
- Over 1,200 injured in Ishikawa, nearly 400 seriously. Tens of thousands forced into emergency shelters.
- More than 170,000 buildings damaged across six prefectures. Houses flattened; roads and ports badly damaged; loss of power and water; transport and supply chains disrupted.
- A tsunami killed two people; early warning and public awareness prevented greater loss. Landslides added to deaths and hazards.
- Economic loss estimated at EUR 9.2 billion to EUR 16.1 billion (the summary says damages up to EUR 17.6 billion). Insurance claims up to EUR 5.5 billion; over 100,000 claims settled by May 2024.
- Environmental: ground uplift up to 5 m changed the coast, creating raised beaches (e.g. Kaiso fishing port lifted out of the water between 2010 and 2024 photos) and damaging farmland and habitats.
Preparation and response in Japan:
- Japan is on the Pacific Ring of Fire; a developed economy with advanced technology, high building standards, public education and detailed earthquake management.
- Short-term: all emergency systems activated; evacuation orders and emergency shelters; automatic shut-off of water, gas and electricity; public transport shut down. Rescue teams use satellite images and drones to check damage, fires and people in need. Expert rescue teams; local volunteers and community groups give emotional and practical support. Public messaging reduces panic and helps families reconnect.
- Long-term: the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) and nationwide seismic network monitor 24/7. The early warning system instantly alerts mobile phones, public speakers, trains and businesses, giving a few seconds to act; trains and lifts stop automatically.
- Strong culture of preparedness: government awareness campaigns, safety manuals, regular drills in schools and workplaces.
- Strict building laws: base isolators, reinforced concrete, steel frames and wood, dampers. Tokyo Skytree and Yokohama Tower use these.
- Regular review: lessons from the 1995 Kobe earthquake led to better communication, stronger buildings and better shelters.
- Outcome: damage and loss of life minimised; quick, safe recovery - a model for the world.

CASE STUDY: SULAWESI EARTHQUAKE, INDONESIA, 2018 (GLOBAL SOUTH)
Cause:
- Indonesia is where three plates meet: the Australian, Philippine and Sunda plates. Sulawesi is where several plates converge.
- On 28 September 2018 a sudden slip on the Palu-Koro Fault (a strike-slip fault that moves about 40 mm per year) caused a magnitude 7.5 earthquake.
- Strike-slip earthquakes rarely cause tsunamis, but bends in the fault and vertical ground shifts triggered a significant tsunami in Palu Bay (waves up to 6 m).
Effects:
- Over 4,300 deaths across Palu, Donggala and other districts. More than 10,000 injured, at least 4,612 seriously. Over 200,000 forced from homes; more than 172,000 later in shelters or temporary housing.
- More than 68,000 homes destroyed or damaged. In Palu and Sigi, liquefaction made whole neighbourhoods sink, with thousands of homes disappearing below the surface. Hundreds of schools, shops, offices and places of worship ruined.
- Economic cost about EUR 840 million, including EUR 790 million infrastructure damage and EUR 132 million lost income (summary: nearly EUR 1 billion).
- Environmental: major soil liquefaction made rescue and rebuilding very hard; the tsunami swept away thousands of coastal buildings.
Preparation and response:
- High risk, but preparedness varies across the country.
- Short-term: evacuation orders; over 140 emergency shelters for 70,000 people; military and Red Cross search and rescue. But damaged roads, collapsed bridges and blocked airports slowed rescue and supplies.
- Technology: drones and satellites mapped damage and found isolated communities; some mobile communication, but power cuts and damaged phone towers made coordination hard.
- Community support: local volunteers, charities and groups gave food, water and emotional support, and searched for trapped victims until official teams arrived.
- Monitoring: the BMKG (Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics) runs monitoring but lacks funding, so it is less efficient. There are tsunami warning buoys and a national network, but many sensors were not working and some sirens failed, so many people had little or no warning.
- Public education: some drills, but awareness much lower than in Japan; many did not know where to go, causing chaos when the tsunami arrived.
- Building codes: exist, especially for public buildings, but many homes in Palu ignored strict standards; few used base isolators, dampers or reinforced frames.
- Review: public anger led BMKG to review and upgrade its warning system and increase investment; calls for more education and better building standards.
- Outcome: brave community action saved lives, but weak buildings and unreliable warnings caused far greater loss than in better-prepared nations.

SUMMARY COMPARISON
- Global North (Japan): strong monitoring, strict codes, rapid response, fewer deaths.
- Global South (Indonesia): weaker infrastructure, higher casualties, slower recovery.
- Key factors: preparedness, building codes, early warning.

rows.prompt: What is the focus of an earthquake?

The point underground where it starts

rows.explanation: Valdivia, magnitude 9.5, is the largest earthquake ever recorded.

rows.prompt: Draw and label a diagram of an earthquake (describe it in words), naming four parts.
rows.model_answer: Deep in the crust is the focus, where the earthquake starts. Seismic waves spread out in rings from the focus and weaken with distance. Directly above the focus on the surface is the epicentre, where shaking is strongest. A fault line runs through the crust to the surface.

rows.prompt: Explain why earthquakes at the Peru-Chile Trench can be both powerful and deep.
rows.model_answer: The denser oceanic Nazca Plate subducts under the continental South American Plate. Rocks bend, twist and break, building friction and stress that is released suddenly as powerful earthquakes. Because they happen all along the sinking plate in the Benioff zone, they range from shallow to deep (up to 700 km).

rows.prompt: Explain how earthquakes happen at a transform plate boundary. Give an example.
rows.model_answer: Two plates slide past each other sideways (shearing). Friction makes them stick, so pressure builds until the shearing force beats the friction and the plates jolt forward, releasing energy. Example: the San Andreas Fault, where the Pacific Plate moves north-west past the North American Plate, causing the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.

rows.prompt: Name and describe two effects of earthquakes.
rows.model_answer: Liquefaction: water-saturated soil loses strength and acts like a liquid, so buildings tilt, sink or collapse, as in Palu. Tsunamis: an underwater earthquake displaces water, sending waves at up to 800 km/h that grow in shallow water and devastate low-lying coasts.

rows.prompt: Outline the difference between short-term and long-term preparation for earthquakes.
rows.model_answer: Short-term preparation is about the moments before, during and just after an earthquake: emergency plans, drills, kits, early warnings and quick rescue. Long-term preparation keeps people safe in the future and helps recovery over months and years, through earthquake-resistant buildings and continuous monitoring.

rows.prompt: Explain how early warning systems reduce the damage caused by earthquakes.
rows.model_answer: Sensors detect shaking and alerts are sent, seconds before strong shaking arrives, to phones, speakers and trains. People can take cover, trains stop and automatic valves shut gas lines and power plants. Shake maps then show emergency services where help is needed most.

rows.prompt: Describe two ways engineers make buildings in Japan earthquake-resistant.
rows.model_answer: Base isolators are flexible pads under buildings that let them move separately from the ground, reducing shaking inside. Dampers absorb vibrations to keep buildings steady, as in the Yokohama Landmark Tower. Flexible materials like steel and wood also bend without breaking.

rows.prompt: Why was the damage in Sulawesi in 2018 worse than it might have been in Japan?
rows.model_answer: Many homes in Palu were built without following strict codes and few used base isolators, dampers or reinforced frames. The warning system lacked funding, so many sensors and sirens failed, and public awareness was low, so people did not know where to go. Damaged roads, bridges and airports also slowed the rescue.

rows.prompt: Explain how earthquakes occur at different types of plate boundary. Refer to examples. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Earthquakes are vibrations of the surface caused by sudden movement along a fault. At convergent boundaries two plates collide, creating intense pressure and stress. The denser oceanic plate subducts under the less dense continental plate, e.g. the Nazca Plate under the South American Plate at the Peru-Chile Trench. Rocks bend, twist and break, creating friction, and stress builds up. When the stress is too great it is released suddenly as energy. These earthquakes happen at many depths in the Benioff zone, from shallow (0-70 km) to deep (300-700 km). The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile (magnitude 9.5) was the largest ever recorded. At divergent boundaries plates move apart, e.g. the Eurasian and North American plates at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The crust stretches and cracks, and magma rises to form new crust. The thin, brittle crust gives frequent, shallow earthquakes under 30 km deep with low magnitude. At transform boundaries plates slide past each other sideways (shearing). Friction makes them stick, and pressure builds until the plates jolt forward. The focus is shallow, so these quakes are very destructive. Example: the San Andreas Fault, where the Pacific Plate moves north-west past the North American Plate, causing the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.
rows.marking_scheme: Three boundary types named/identified (credit within SRPs). Named examples 2m x 2 (e.g. Peru-Chile Trench, Mid-Atlantic Ridge, San Andreas Fault). Explanation: 13 SRPs x 2m = 26m, e.g. collision/pressure; denser plate subducts; friction and stress; sudden release; Benioff zone depths; Valdivia 9.5; plates move apart; crust stretches/cracks; magma rises; shallow under 30 km, low magnitude; shearing; plates stick and jolt; shallow focus, destructive; 1906 San Francisco. Max 4 marks for a single boundary type if only one is developed in full. Total 30 marks.

rows.prompt: Assess the preparation for and response to an earthquake in a Global North setting that you have studied. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Global North example: Noto earthquake, Japan, January 2024 (magnitude 7.6). Japan lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire, and as a developed economy has invested heavily in preparation. Long term, the Japan Meteorological Agency and a nationwide seismic network monitor earthquakes 24 hours a day. The early warning system instantly sends alerts to mobile phones, public speakers, trains and businesses, giving a few seconds to act, and trains and lifts stop automatically. Strict building laws require base isolators, reinforced concrete, steel frames, wood and dampers, as in the Tokyo Skytree. There is a strong culture of preparedness, with government awareness campaigns, safety manuals and regular drills in schools and workplaces. Japan reviews its plans after each disaster; lessons from the 1995 Kobe earthquake improved communication, buildings and shelters. In the short-term response, emergency systems were activated, people were evacuated to shelters and gas, water and electricity were shut off automatically. Rescue teams used satellite images and drones to find damage and people in need, while volunteers gave practical and emotional support. Tsunami warnings meant only two people died in the tsunami. However, at least 645 people died, many when older homes collapsed, and over 170,000 buildings were damaged, so preparation could not prevent all losses. Overall, Japan's preparation and response greatly reduced loss of life, making it a world model.
rows.marking_scheme: Named Global North example 2m. Assessment: 14 SRPs x 2m = 28m, covering both preparation and response (max 10 SRPs on one aspect). Credit e.g. JMA 24/7 monitoring; early warning to phones/trains; automatic stops; base isolators; dampers; flexible materials; Tokyo Skytree/Yokohama Tower; drills and campaigns; review after Kobe 1995; evacuation and shelters; automatic shut-offs; drones/satellites; volunteers; tsunami warning saved lives; statistics 645 deaths/170,000 buildings; evaluative judgement. Total 30 marks.

rows.prompt: With reference to a Global South example you have studied, examine the effects of an earthquake. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Example: the Sulawesi earthquake, Indonesia, 28 September 2018, magnitude 7.5 on the Palu-Koro strike-slip fault. Human effects were severe: over 4,300 people died across Palu, Donggala and other districts, more than 10,000 were injured and over 200,000 were forced from their homes. More than 68,000 homes were destroyed or damaged. Liquefaction in Palu and Sigi made whole neighbourhoods sink, with thousands of homes vanishing below the surface. A tsunami with waves up to 6 m hit Palu Bay, sweeping away thousands of coastal buildings. Hundreds of schools, shops, offices and places of worship were ruined. The economic cost was about EUR 840 million, including EUR 790 million of infrastructure damage. Damaged roads, bridges and airports slowed rescue and aid.
rows.marking_scheme: Named example 2m. Examination: 9 SRPs x 2m = 18m, e.g. deaths 4,300+; 10,000 injured; 200,000 displaced; 68,000 homes; liquefaction in Palu/Sigi; tsunami up to 6 m; schools/services destroyed; economic cost EUR 840 million; infrastructure damage slowed aid; shelters for 172,000. Total 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain how scientists monitor seismic activity and how this helps to reduce the effects of earthquakes. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Seismometers are placed in the ground to detect and record vibrations, converting them into electrical signals shown as seismograms. Modern seismometers use three sensors to measure up-down, east-west and north-south movement, giving precise location and magnitude. Seismic networks link many seismometers across regions, such as the US Geological Survey, giving real-time, more accurate data. Accelerometers measure how quickly the ground moves, helping to assess damage. Satellites detect ground shifts, cracks and deformation from space. Computers rapidly analyse this data, and GIS gives interactive maps. This monitoring feeds early warning systems, which send alerts seconds before shaking, so people take cover, trains stop and gas lines shut. Shake maps help emergency services prioritise rescue.

Total 20 marks.
